My name is Mark. I've spent years diving deep into financial markets, behavioral economics, and the money systems that quietly shape our lives — so you can skip the hard part. My goal is to turn complicated money topics into simple, animated breakdowns that actually make sense and stick with you. School taught us the Pythagorean theorem but never mentioned compound interest, emergency funds, or how credit cards really make their money. If you're done living paycheck to paycheck and ready to learn how money actually works, welcome — you're exactly who I made this channel for.

🔔 Subscribe now. The best time to start was yesterday. The second best time is right now.

text:
Investing $100 a month sounds too small to matter, until you see what it does through a bad year. Dev put $100 a month into an S&P 500 index fund in January 2000, one of the worst starting dates in modern market history, and watched his account fall below what he had put in, not once but twice. He never stopped. Twenty-five years later he had put in $30,000 and his account held about $146,000.

Two friends started with the same $100. Cora waited for the dust to settle and began in 2003, finishing about $27,700 behind Dev. Pete started the same day Dev did, sold at the end of 2008, and finished about $134,000 behind without making a single bad trade. Same $100. Same fund. Three completely different lives. Here is the real math behind why.

But the numbers hold an uncomfortable surprise. For Dev's first ten years, a plain 2% savings account would have beaten the stock market, about $13,300 against $12,634. More than 90% of what he ended up with arrived after the point where the plan looked like a failure.

In this video: what Dev's account looked like at its worst, what he was really holding while the balance was falling, why a crash lets the same $100 buy more shares, how Lila, who started at the 2009 bottom, still finished with less than half of Dev's total, the moment Pete turned a temporary loss into a permanent one, how a 1% fund fee takes about $19,000 from the same $100, where your first $100 should go, how to find it in forgotten subscriptions, the one kind of money that should never go into stocks, why $146,000 is a start and not a retirement, and the one sentence to write down before the next crash.

Figures come from the calendar-year returns of the S&P 500 with dividends included, spread evenly across each year, and are not adjusted for inflation. Real results would differ somewhat. This is a history lesson, not a forecast. This video is for education and entertainment only and is not financial advice.
